title: NASA's Sharp-Eyed Satellite Catches a Colossal Ocean Swell That Could Unleash El Niño
summary: A sprawling mound of warm water, hundreds of miles wide, is creeping across the Pacific—and NASA's most precise sea-level satellite just caught it in the act. The Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich mission, a joint U.S.-European effort, detected a Kelvin wave that has now reached the coast of South America. Sea levels near Peru were more than 5.9 inches (15 centimeters) above average by mid-May, a telltale sign of building ocean heat. Because water expands as it warms, these bulges reveal where temperatures are rising beneath the surface. Kelvin waves are often the opening act of El Niño, a climate phenomenon that can disrupt weather worldwide. They begin when westerly wind bursts in the far western Pacific push warm water eastward. If several such waves stack up over months, they can trigger a full-blown El Niño, characterized by unusually warm sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. "While this year's event started a bit later than the big El Niños of 2015 and 1997, it's beginning to catch up," said Josh Willis, a sea level researcher at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. The consequences can be severe. El Niño shifts the jet stream, altering storm tracks and rainfall patterns. The 2015-2016 event contributed to drought in Africa and flooding in California. Even moderate El Niños, like those in 2018 and 2023, caused regional droughts and floods. "Every El Niño is different," noted JPL's Severine Fournier. "But they almost always make for a hot year and big changes in rainfall in parts of the globe." The satellite, named after former NASA Earth Science Director Michael Freilich, measures sea surface height every 10 days with inch-level precision. It continues a climate record started in 1992 by TOPEX/Poseidon. Its successor, Sentinel-6B, launched in late 2025 and will take over by end of 2026. For now, scientists are watching closely. El Niño typically peaks between November and January, so the full picture won't emerge for months. As Nadya Vinogradova Shiffer of NASA Headquarters put it, "Stay tuned as more ocean stories continue to unfold."
why_it_matters: Recognizing early signs like Kelvin waves can give countries months to prepare for floods, droughts, and heat waves, making food and water supplies more secure for a generation that will face more weather extremes.

background_read: The warm-water pulse spotted by Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich (a satellite launched in 2020 to track sea levels to within an inch) is a classic early signal of El Niño, part of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO).
Fishermen off Peru named 'El Niño' (Spanish for 'the little boy') centuries ago when they noticed the ocean warming around Christmas.

Since 1992, a series of NASA-CNES satellites—starting with TOPEX/Poseidon—have measured global sea surface height with radar, catching several strong El Niños, including the massive 1997 and 2015 events that caused billions in damage.

The new data from the Freilich satellite (named after former NASA Earth Science Director Michael Freilich) joins this archive, helping scientists at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory refine their predictions.
Understanding these ocean bulges from space gives a months-long warning for droughts, floods and heat waves, a critical head start in a warming world.

perspectives.description: Farmers, water managers, and disaster agencies could get earlier warnings, letting them shift planting schedules or shore up reservoirs. Better El Niño forecasts can save lives and reduce economic losses.

Satellite data can miss local weather quirks, and El Niño forecasts are still imperfect; false alarms or missed signals can lead to wasted resources or unexpected disasters. Furthermore, natural variability will always surprise us.

El Niño is a natural oscillation that has shaped climate for millennia; satellites now give a systematic, long-term view that older ship logs couldn't match. Yet the raw data still needs skilful interpretation to become actionable information.

With Sentinel-6B and future missions, scientists aim to push forecast lead times even further. The next step is translating ocean bulges into hyper-local forecasts that can be delivered straight to a farmer's phone.
